newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 18.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 18.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Tuesday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* President Clinton stopped the pilots' strike at AMR's American Airlines after intense lobbying, and minutes after he signed the order, American announced a 50-percent fare sale.
* People close to the talks say union leaders for the pilots at American Airlines are willing to compromise over who will fly the company's smaller jets if American raises its financial offer.
* HealthSouth could announce as early as today a pact to acquire Horizon/CMS Healthcare in a stock swap worth about $950 million, plus the assumption of debt.
* Corporate profits rose 61 percent in the fourth quarter, according to a Wall Street Journal tabulation.
* Some members of Congress are supporting a new airline tax tied to fuel use as an alternative to the 10 percent ticket tax and user-fee plan.
* Sixty-nine countries signed a global telecommunications pact designed to open up new markets for the industry.
* Stone-Consolidated and Abitibi-Price agreed to merge in a deal valued at about $1.5 billion, creating the world's largest newsprint maker.
* After 19 months, six striking Detroit unions agreed to return to work at Gannett Co's Detroit News and Knight-Ridder's Detroit Free Press.
* Wholesale prices fell 0.3 percent in January after rising 0.6 percent in December.
* Freeport-McMoran Copper won the right to build and operate what is believed to be the world's largest gold discovery, the Busang gold discovery in the Indonesian portion of Borneo.
* Staples began an advertising campaign to convince customers and regulators that its acquistion of Office Depot will lower prices.
* CompuServe Chief Executive Robert Massey resigned.
* The Securities and Exchange Commission charged Centennial Technologies Chief Executive Emanuel Pinez with insider trading and fraud.

* Wall Streeters, after losing hundreds of millions of dollars as Ronald Perelman dragged Marvel Entertainment Group into bankruptcy court, now are rejoicing over every small setback for the billionaire. -- Heard on the Street.

* Say goodbye to easy pickings in the asset-backed securities market. Investors once had little to do but choose a basket of asset-backed securities, plunk their money down and wait for the profits to flow. The cumulative return for asset-backed securities during the past three years was 26.5 percent, compared with a 23.6 percent return for Treasury securities of similar maturities.

Times have changed. Sudden difficulties at auto lenders Jayhawk Acceptance Corp and Mercury Finance, as well as concerns about Banc One Corp, Cargill Inc's Access Financial and Mitsubishi Motors Corp have sent some prices down and forced investors to scrutinize issuers of asset-backed securities like never before. -- Credit Markets.
